title: In the classroom
goal: Say where things are, use prepositions correctly, and understand why the word after a preposition always changes its final vowel.
bekal: say where things are with *fii*, *'alaa*, *tahta*, *amaama* and friends
ask where something is with *aina* and give a full answer
recognize the kasra that appears after a preposition

dialogs.title: حِوَار — أَيْنَ الْقَامُوسُ؟
dialogs.intro: Just before class starts. Budi has lost his dictionary.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا، اَلطَّاوِلَةُ فَارِغَةٌ. عَلَيْهَا كِتَابٌ فَقَطْ.
lines.id: No, the table is empty. There's only a book on it.
lines.literal: no, the-table empty. on-it book only.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Have a look under the chair.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا شَيْءَ هُنَاكَ. رُبَّمَا فِي حَقِيبَتِي؟
lines.baca: laa shai'a hunaak. rubbamaa fii haqiibatii?
lines.id: There's nothing there. Maybe it's in my bag?
lines.literal: no thing there. perhaps in bag-my?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: هِيَ خَلْفَ الْبَابِ، بَيْنَ الْجِدَارِ وَالْخِزَانَةِ.
lines.id: Behind the door, between the wall and the cupboard.
lines.literal: it behind the-door, between the-wall and-the-cupboard.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: هَا هُوَ الْقَامُوسُ! إِنَّهُ دَاخِلَ الْحَقِيبَةِ.
lines.id: There it is! It's inside the bag.
lines.literal: here it the-dictionary! indeed-it inside the-bag.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.literal: the praise to God! thanks plenty.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: You're welcome. The teacher is at the door now.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Come on! The lesson is starting.

notes: **يَا marks direct address.** When you call someone by name, it is almost always preceded by يَا: يَا لَيْلَى, يَا أُسْتَاذ, يَا أَخِي. Leaving it out sounds clipped, like calling someone without any tone. English has no real equivalent — the old "O" (as in "O Lord") is the closest, but يَا is completely neutral and everyday.

**The word after a preposition always takes a kasra.** عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ (not الطَّاوِلَةُ), فِي الْبَيْتِ, تَحْتَ الْكُرْسِيِّ. This is the one part of case endings you really need to use actively at A1, because you can clearly hear it at the end of a sentence.

**عَلَيْهَا — a preposition merged with a pronoun.** عَلَى + هَا = عَلَيْهَا ("on it"). Likewise فِي + هِ = فِيهِ, مَعَ + كَ = مَعَكَ, لِ + ي = لِي. Notice that عَلَى and إِلَى change to عَلَيْ and إِلَيْ before an ending is attached.

**تَحْتَ, أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ are always followed directly by a noun.** They are really nouns used as adverbs, so the combination is an idafa: تَحْتَ الْكُرْسِيِّ = "the underside of the chair". That's why the next word takes a kasra, just like the idafa in unit 4.

**بَيْنَ needs two things, joined with وَ.** بَيْنَ الْجِدَارِ وَالْخِزَانَةِ ("between the wall and the cupboard"). If the second one is a pronoun, وَ is still used: بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ ("between me and you") — notice that بَيْنَ is repeated; using it only once is not allowed.
**هَا هُوَ — "there it is".** Used exactly like the English phrase when you find something: هَا هُوَ (masculine), هَا هِيَ (feminine). Very common in conversation.

**إِنَّ adds emphasis.** إِنَّهُ دَاخِلَ الْحَقِيبَةِ is roughly "it's indeed inside the bag". إِنَّ is always followed by a noun or an attached pronoun, and it makes a sentence sound firmer and more formal. You'll find it constantly in the news.

**لَا شَيْءَ** literally "no thing". You've already seen this pattern — لَا + a noun without tanween — in لَا مُشْكِلَةَ (unit 2). It states total absence, and it is very often used on its own as an answer: "nothing".
**هَيَّا بِنَا** is the Arabic "let's go!", used to get people moving together. The short form is just هَيَّا.

grammars.title: Prepositions and words of place
after: The difference between فَوْقَ and عَلَى is exactly "above" versus "on": كِتَابٌ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ (a book on the table), اَلطَّائِرَةُ فَوْقَ الْمَدِينَةِ (the plane above the city). In everyday speech the line is often blurry.
خَلْفَ and وَرَاءَ mean the same. وَرَاءَ sounds a little more literary; خَلْفَ is more common in conversation.

grammars.title: Prepositions merged with pronouns
after: This table looks dense, but you've already used half of it without noticing: عِنْدِي (unit 4), لَكِ (unit 3), بِنَا (the dialogue you just read). Only two things need attention: **عَلَى and إِلَى become عَلَيْ and إِلَيْ**, and **لِ becomes لَ** for every form except لِي.

sections.title: In the classroom and at home

blocks.text: Notice the مَ- in مَطْبَخ, مَكْتَب, مَدْرَسَة, مَكْتَبَة: that prefix marks a **place**. مَكْتَب from the root ك-ت-ب (write) = place for writing; مَطْبَخ from ط-ب-خ (cook) = place for cooking; مَدْرَسَة from د-ر-س (study) = place for studying. Once you see the pattern, dozens of words become guessable.

blocks.title: Three-letter roots: the biggest time-saver
items: Almost every Arabic word grows out of three consonants carrying one basic meaning. ك-ت-ب means "write": كَتَبَ (he wrote), كِتَاب (book), كَاتِب (writer), مَكْتَب (desk), مَكْتَبَة (library), مَكْتُوب (written).
From now on, every time you meet a new word, try to spot its three consonants. Not to memorize as a rule, but so that new words stop feeling random and start feeling related.

blocks.text: Look at the last row: Arabic can flip a nominal sentence and put the place first — عَلَيْهَا كِتَابٌ, literally "on it (is) a book". This isn't a stylistic choice but a **requirement** when the thing being talked about is indefinite. The sentence كِتَابٌ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ sounds lopsided to Arab ears.

The same pattern is used to say something exists: هُنَاكَ كِتَابٌ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ ("there is a book on the table"). In that position هُنَاكَ no longer means "over there" but "there is" — exactly like English *there is*.

blocks.title: One sentence, two meanings — careful
items: اَلْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ = "the book is on the table" (says where a known book is).
عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ = "on the table there is a book" (announces that a book is there).
English tells them apart with "there is"; Arabic tells them apart by **word order** and by whether the noun is definite.

exercises.prompt: Join the preposition with the pronoun given.

items: The bag is behind the door.
There's a book on the table.
The teacher is in front of the blackboard.

exercises.prompt: Answer about the room you're sitting in right now. Full sentences.

answers: عَلَى — تَحْتَ — أَمَامَ — فِي / دَاخِلَ — قُرْبَ — بَيْنَ
عَلَيْهَا — فِيهِ — مَعَكَ — إِلَيْهِمْ — لَهَا — مِنَّا
أَيْنَ قَامُوسِي؟ — اَلْحَقِيبَةُ خَلْفَ الْبَابِ. — عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ. — اَلْمُدَرِّسُ أَمَامَ السَّبُّورَةِ. — أَسْكُنُ فِي جَاكَرْتَا. — لَا شَيْءَ دَاخِلَ الْخِزَانَةِ.
Example: اَلْبَابُ خَلْفِي. — اَلنَّافِذَةُ بِجَانِبِي. — عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ وَقَلَمٌ. — تَحْتَ الْكُرْسِيِّ حَقِيبَتِي. — نَعَمْ، عِنْدِي قَامُوسٌ.
